## Skills are to LLMs what packages are to programming languages

The more I use CLI LLM tools like Claude Code and Opencode, the more I realise that :
- the skills specification is one of the best ideas I've seen and used until now
- it does exactly what packages do with my favourite languages : factorise some cool stuff into reusable chunks that I can call with very few words
- it's still not mature and it should definatly evolve to behave like packages

I've been experimenting with ideas that revolve around this skills as packages approximation and I like the current results enough that I want to talk about it, if only to read it back again in a few months and see how bad this take is.

## Skills are such a good idea

LLM Skills, as in the [open specification](https://agentskills.io/home) for a reusable prompt format, are CLEVER.
Everyone was playing around with prompt engineering and reusing bits that worked in larger and larger prompts, copy and pasting things, cross referencing structural documents. Skills deliver on all fronts : progressive disclosure lets us save some context for the good stuff before landing in the [dumb zone](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rmvDxxNubIg), self-activation means we don't have to waste turns or tokens naming the invocation, and the folder structure means we can have even more progressive disclosure, with files read only in certain situations, scripts used as part of the skill ...

Right after codifying actions, skills are the best option for reproducibility of good output (or at least, the output you expect from a task).

I daily drive 4 tools : Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Mistral Vibe and OpenCode. They all support skills. So do at least 30 others like Cursor, Kimi Code CLI, Antigravity, Cline, Codex, Gemini CLI and all the others that I can't name but know exist.
If that's not a consensus, I don't know what is.

I'm used close to a 100 different of them at the time of writing, I'd say around 80 found online and 10 to 20 tailor built for a repo / situation. They help push the agent towards working methodologies like lean, tdd, how to write ADRs, how to review code, how to use a specific R or JS package ... They work !
My favourite home-made, which truly means "my version of what everyone and their dog is also making", are solve-issue, planning-team and implementing-team : 3 skills that work together at solving an issue on the repo's Github page by writing a specification with me, then using subagents and team driven agent orchestration to derive a plan, make a few rounds of review, then wait for me to read and then implement / review in rounds again, all in a single session. I still get a shot of dopamine each time I see the agents trigger the skills, or when I get a full new feature after an hours long session ends and it's one-shot right or close to it.

## Skill management needs to mature

**a) Growth without management.**

The first thing that bothered me happened because I'm a hoarder : I was downloading skills left and right, and asking Opus to make a lot of them from books/blogs and package documentation of my favourite packages, "to have them just in case".
Suddenly, I land on a [skill aggregator](skillsmp.com/) which states that it's found 200k+ skills !
Even with progressive disclosure, at a stupidly impossible 1 tok/skill that's still more tokens than Opus' context window, twice it's "smart window" !
Even though I was FAR from flooding the LLM's context with my < 100 skills, it now felt like I was doing something unsustainable.

**b) Staleness.**

Another issue that arose even more quickly : staleness.
Between [superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers)[^1] that kept growing, but only updated automatically in Claude Code (thanks to the marketplace installation), my own skills evolving each session, my repos quickly ended up having different versions of the same skills, and I couldn't track what was where or what was working/not.

[^1]: If you don't know about that one you're misssing something crucial. The brainstorming skill is probably the single most value-adding skill I've used yet
**c) Distribution across tools.**

In addition, all these skills had to be copy pasted in the appropriate places : .claude, .github, wait no that's .agents, wait I want it globally, wait no it's creating confusion in that repo, WAIT this machine has none of my global skills !!
The frustration of manually managing all of this really triggered my nerd reflex of trying to [automate the thing](https://xkcd.com/1319/).

**d) Git pollution vs. reproducibility.**

Last, but not least maybe, I have conflicting feelings about repo-local skills. I can make the case for skills being in the repo, to let others know how you've used LLMs to generate code or documentation. But I also find it quite annoying how different and noisy it is to the rest of the codebase. I don't think I need to have the full spec committed to 4 different folders in my repo just because I test drive 4 CLI tools. I should be able to declare the skills I use in a compact and standardized format.

## Wait : isn't this just what package managers are for ?

*Why is it February 2026 and nobody has built this yet? Is it because it's too early (not enough skills in the wild), too fragmented (every tool has its own format), or just because nobody's been bothered enough?*

It's a weird feeling for me to try and build something that, to my current knowledge, nobody had already built and distributed globally.
I'm at a point in my developper evolution that I no longer forget that open source exists and waste[^2] hours and days either reinventing the wheel or somehow accepting to suffer through a task that someone had generously wrapped in a package somewhere.
No, I now know to quickly say "hey it would be cool if I could have this done this way, let's search through Google and Github" and usually land on something cool, very often with tens of thousands of Github stars, showing me again and again how much is out there that I don't know about.
I don't know how that stage is called, not a newborn anymore but not too far from it ?

Anyway, the only thing I found when I started tinkering with automated skill management around mid-january (repo says 13/01 for first commit) was ... nothing. I mean, the marketplace thing in Claude Code was nice, but I mean open-source and tool-agnostic solution.

About 2 weeks ago I finally noticed (thanks to SkillsMP) that `[npx skills]`(https://www.npmjs.com/package/skills?activeTab=readme) existed, and this one is really cool ! It solved quite a few of the issues I was having, especially ditribution across many CLI tools (they support ~40 !!!), updating and tracking from source, global/local management.

But there was still the issue of growing collection of skills, and repo-pollution.

[^2]: I say waste but I have to admit that's more often than not quite a useful learning experience to spend some time tinkering with the problem without knowing a ready-made solution exists

## My take : skillverse

**a) Cold storage.**

So, the first thing I built was a cold-storage for skills.
It's quite simple : skills are stored in .local/share/llm-skills in each machine, single copy, CLI-tool invisible.

I then generate a library.json file from the assortment of folders, and I can add variables to each skill : is it destined to the global folder (core: true) ? What are it's tags (for search) ?

Then it's all bash scripts and 3 layers of skill activation :

### Layer 1

Another script symlinks the core skills to the global skills directories for my 4 tools

My growing collection is managed in a git repo, and I use it as the central source of truth across machines (library.json included), so that on each machine I only need to run a "sync" bash script to update from the remote and rebuild the symlinks.

### Layer 2

At the repo level, I'm quite proud of the current iteration :

- I have a wrapper around the entrypoint each CLI tool (claude() etc) that creates a temporary directory and passes it to the `--add-dir` argument, then reads a manifest file in the repo that declares the skills to activate in that repo and symlinks then to the temp-dir. When I exit the session, the temp-dir is deleted. I can add/remove

**b) Three-layer activation.**
**c) Symlinks, not copies.**
**d) A CLI to manage it all.**

## From me to me (6 months from now)

*If you re-read this post in a year, what do you want to have been right about?*



Skills are such a good idea.
Skills are here to stay. The Skills spec[] is clever, progressive disclosure is really what was needed.
Skills are to the LLM what packages are to your programming language of choice (unless you're writing C apparently)

Skills factorise common operations you like into a shorter interface. It's a good-enough attempt at providing more reproducibility to LLM outputs.
Skills are supported by most of the tools out there : OpenCode, Mistral Vibe, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI ...

Currently, skills can be located in your global folder (say, ~/.claude/skills or ~/.agents/skills), or in your local repo.
Some tools like Claude Code support an --add-dir argument to specify another folder to add to the session, and if this folder contains skills they are added to the context.

Current issues :
- Growing libraries of skills. They will grow naturally. We all like to hoard : install <pkg> just to test and then forget about your global machine library. But current solutions like npx skills Vercel add the skills either to global or local. No "unactivated" skills anywhere.
- Skills going stale : npx skills does that well. I don't know if it tracks in-repo skills well but at least it updates global skills, I've tried it.
- Skills distribution : if you are testing many CLI tools (they change all the time), you need skills in .claude, .agents, .vibe ...
- Git pollution : your global skills influence the LLM output but you're not committing them to the repo. Why would you want to commit some inside the repo ? You want skills that operate at the repo level, because your R skills are useless in your Rust crate, but they are here to affect the LLM behavior. I understand and share the need to tell others that LLMs are working on this repo and which skills they are using, but do you need to share the full text ? It's not really a good fit amongst the commits that change / fix and otherwise progress your project

Solutions :

- A cold storage : a central source of truth, a place where you can access skills you need at any time, but not activated (in context for the LLM). Managed by a program, with metadata to power skills search, discovery, update, adding and removing, and publishing (you can make skills faster than packages !)
- A declarative file for skills dependencies : like packages, we can have a file that tells others what we use, maybe even which revision.
- Using a staging fleeting folder : when you run claude() or vibe(), add a folder that reads the skills-deps file and adds the skills to that folder. Not seen by git, but in context for the llm.
- Commands to update your skills, like with packages.

Where I am now : rplsmn/shared-safe-config (rename !)

I have :

- A machine setup script that installs Claude Code, Open Code, Mistral Vibe, Copilot CLI and wrappers around their entrypoints add start and stop hooks.
  - on startup, 2 directories are added : 1) the ARTIFACTS_DIR where agents store their ... artifacts ! That means plans, specs, reserach reports etc and 2) a temporary (lifetime = session) dir where local skills are symlinked depending on a manifest file in the repo
  - on exit, the artifact dir makes a commit, and pushes to the remote, the temp-dir is destroyed.
- A registry that saves skills and agents to a central location and serves symlinks to the relevant folders for all 4 tools
- A script to automate the distribution of global scripts via a library.json file where core:true means the skill goes to global, and the rest is cold
- A bash tool that can :
  - Add / remove a local skill to a repo via a symlink ; tracked only by a manifest file in the repo
  - List skills available on the machine, and their activation state
  - Add / remove *temporary* skills to the temporary session dir (without editing the manifest)
  - Synchronise the global library when the registry changes
  - Promote a skill to the registry when it's mature

I want to add :

- Adding a skill found in the while, starting with github repo
- Managing skills versions, and their origin, for update / retrograde from the cli
- Declaring skill dependencies on each other
- A proper search interface + function for finding skills in a repo + and auto add based on patterns in the repo (R markers, cargo.toml, env descriptions ...)
- Extract the management of my gitconfig to another tool !!
